title: Control weeds pests and plant diseases in an agricultural field using chemicals

lessons.title: Knowing the problem and the chemical
lessons.html:
Weeds, pests and diseases

Crops such as maize, wheat, potatoes, soya beans and vegetables are attacked by three main problems:

  • Weeds: unwanted plants that steal water, light and food from the crop, for example khakibos and nutgrass.
  • Pests: insects and other animals that eat or damage the crop, such as stalk borer, aphids, bollworm and cutworm.
  • Diseases: caused by fungi, bacteria or viruses, such as rust, blight and leaf spots.

Chemicals used against them are called agricultural remedies or pesticides: herbicides for weeds, insecticides for insects and fungicides for fungal diseases. In South Africa these products must be registered under Act 36 of 1947 (the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act). Only registered products may be used, and only on the crops and pests on the label.

Scouting first

Before spraying, the field is scouted: someone walks the field, looks for weeds, pests and disease, counts them and writes it down. The manager then decides if spraying is needed. Spraying only when needed saves money, protects useful insects such as bees and ladybirds, and slows down resistance.

The label is the law

Every product has a label. Read it, or have it read to you, before you work with the product. The label tells you:

  • Which crops and problems it is registered for.
  • The dose (how much product per hectare or per tank).
  • Mixing instructions and what it may be mixed with.
  • The PPE you must wear.
  • The re-entry period (when people may go back into the field) and the withholding period (how long before harvest you may not spray).
  • First aid instructions and the poison warning colour band.

Never guess a dose. Follow the label and your supervisor's spray instruction.

lessons.title: Mixing and applying chemicals safely
lessons.html:
Before you spray

  1. Get a written spray instruction: field, crop, product, dose, water volume and date.
  2. Check the sprayer: no leaks, nozzles clean and the right type, filters clean, pressure gauge working. The sprayer must be calibrated so it sprays the right amount.
  3. Put on PPE as the label says: chemical-resistant gloves, overall, rubber boots, face shield or goggles and a respirator if needed.
  4. Check the weather. Do not spray in strong wind, when rain is coming, or in the heat of the day.

Mixing

  • Mix in the open air or a well-ventilated mixing area, away from water sources.
  • Half-fill the tank with clean water, add the measured product, then fill up while the agitator runs.
  • Use a measuring jug kept only for chemicals.
  • Triple-rinse empty containers and pour the rinse water into the tank.

Applying

  • Drive or walk at a steady speed so the spray is even.
  • Do not spray over dams, rivers, homes or neighbouring crops. Watch for drift.
  • Keep people and animals out of the field.
  • Put up warning signs if the farm uses them, and keep to the re-entry period.

Never do this

  • Never eat, drink or smoke while working with chemicals.
  • Never blow out a blocked nozzle with your mouth.
  • Never use empty containers for water or food.
  • Never wash the sprayer in a river or dam.

After spraying

Wash the sprayer in the set place. Wash PPE separately from other clothes. Shower. Record the date, field, product, dose, area sprayed, weather and your name.

If someone is poisoned

Remove the person from the area, take off contaminated clothes, wash skin with plenty of water, and get medical help quickly. Take the label with you to the clinic or hospital. Follow the label first aid instructions.

Key points

  • Scout first and spray only when the manager decides it is needed.
  • Only use registered products and follow the label exactly.
  • Wear the PPE on the label and check the sprayer and weather.
  • Never eat, drink or smoke while spraying, and never spray near water.
  • Record every application and keep to re-entry and withholding periods.
